other_side: NLW's lead is that the argument has moved from whether AI is real to how to do it well, and that companies are working the second-order problems — token budgets, writing policies, de-skilling — quickly and in public. Zitron's most recent free piece argues that this sophistication is beside the point if the paying demand it implies never turns up in the vendors' own numbers. He puts Microsoft's fiscal 2026 AI revenue at roughly $34.4 billion, of which about $24.1 billion is OpenAI's own compute spend, leaving around $10.3 billion from every other AI product Microsoft sells, against $261.3 billion of capital expenditure since 2022 — "$10.33 billion in annual revenue is a catastrophic failure." His inference is blunt: "If Microsoft doesn't have the demand, nobody has the demand," and the enterprise playbooks being shared so enthusiastically are a story the market tells itself rather than a line of revenue anyone can point at.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether enterprise AI use converts into money — real, paid, non-lab demand. They accept more in common than the framing suggests: that inference carries a genuine marginal cost, that firms have exhausted annual budgets in months, and that the two frontier labs account for most of what is currently being spent on compute. The empirical question is what non-lab enterprise AI revenue does over the next year, and the observable that settles it is hyperscaler AI revenue reported separately from OpenAI's and Anthropic's own compute purchases. Whittemore is vindicated if that residual line grows sharply while firms raise budgets on measured returns; Zitron if it stays near ten billion for Microsoft while capital expenditure climbs. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is what they agree on despite opposite priors: tokens are an operating expense and value has to be shown per unit. Watch the next quarter's disclosure of AI revenue apart from lab compute.
